title: Documenting the capstone design
idea: Design documentation is the short set of diagrams and contract comments that lets another engineer understand, use and change your system without asking you.
points: A class diagram shows structure: types, key members, and their dependencies.
A sequence diagram shows one use case in time, like one `book` call.
Javadoc states each method's contract: inputs, units, edge cases, and error codes thrown.
Keep diagrams as text beside the code, so reviews show diagram changes too.

messages.note: Dashed arrows are returns. Draw them only when the value matters to the story.

messages.note: No clash. On true, the diagram would end here with `RoomTakenException`.

messages.note: The save happens before any listener runs: the order is a design decision worth showing.

code.title: Class diagram as Mermaid
code.caption: The capstone's structure as Mermaid text. Kept in the repository, it renders inside a mermaid code block on GitHub or GitLab.

walk.text: Show fields that are dependencies, and public methods with types. Skip getters and private helpers.
The `<<interface>>` label tells the reader this is an extension point, not a concrete class.
Filled diamond is composition: rooms belong to one building and do not exist without it.
Plain arrows are associations the service holds as fields. `*` means any number of listeners.
Dotted arrows with a hollow head mean implements: two Observers of one interface.

code.title: Javadoc with a runnable demo
code.caption: The contract in Javadoc, and a `main` that runs each documented case so a reviewer can compare output with the docs.

walk.text: The class comment fixes the unit once. Every reader now knows 9.5 means 09:30.
State the edge case in words: half-open slots, so touching bookings do not clash.
Each `@throws` names an exception with a stable code. Callers can rely on these.
Short methods still list every failure, including an unknown id: `IllegalArgumentException`.
Each documented case runs here, back-to-back included. A reviewer compares this output with the docs.

pitfalls: Drawing every getter and private field hides the dependencies the reader actually needs.
Diagrams saved as images go stale; keep Mermaid text in the repository next to the code.
Javadoc that repeats the method name adds nothing; document units, edge cases and exceptions.

quiz.q: A reviewer must see why a cancelled booking still sent an email. Which diagram helps most?
options: A class diagram of every capstone type
A sequence diagram of the `cancel` use case
A use case diagram listing all actors
A package diagram of the modules
quiz.why: The question is about the order of calls in one flow. Only a sequence diagram shows order; the others show structure or scope.

takeaway: Draw structure once, draw each key flow in time, and document every contract.
